expectedText:
CERTIFICATE OF AMENDMENT TO ARTICLES OF INCORPORATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Corp

CERTIFICATE OF AMENDMENT DECLARATION
The name of the corporation is Acme Corp. The corporation's name immediately before this amendment, if this amendment changes the corporate name, was Acme Inc. The following amendment to the articles of incorporation of Acme Corp has been adopted: ARTICLE I: The name of the corporation is Acme Corp. This amendment has been approved by the board of directors of Acme Corp and, to the extent approval by the outstanding shares is required by law, has also been approved by the required vote of the outstanding shares of Acme Corp entitled to vote on it.

THE GENERAL POWER TO AMEND ARTICLES OF INCORPORATION
California's amendment-of-articles chapter gives every corporation a broad, standing statutory power to change its own articles after formation: by following that chapter's procedures, a corporation may amend its articles from time to time, in any and as many respects as desired, so long as the articles as amended contain only provisions that would be lawful to insert in original articles filed at the time of the amendment. The Legislature intended this power to reach the fullest extent of the state's reserved authority over corporations, and the power applies even if a provision in the amendment would not have been permissible when the corporation was originally incorporated. That broad power has one narrow carve-out: a corporation cannot use an amendment to add or alter the original articles' historical statements of its initial street and mailing address, the names and addresses of its first directors, or the name and address of its initial agent for service of process -- except to correct an error in one of those statements, or to delete that information entirely once the corporation has since filed a statement of information under a separate statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "By complying with the provisions of this chapter, a corporation may amend its articles from time to time, in any and as many respects as may be desired, so long as its articles as amended contain only such provisions as it would be lawful to insert in original articles filed at the time of the filing of the amendment"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 900(a), California General Corporation Law, the general power to amend articles (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=900.)
  "A corporation shall not amend its articles to add any statement or to alter any statement that may appear in the original articles of the initial street address and initial mailing address of the corporation, the names and addresses of the first directors, or the name and address of the initial agent, except to correct an error in the statement or to delete the information after the corporation has filed a statement under Section 1502."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 900(b), California General Corporation Law, the historical-information carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=900.)
  Known gap: A premise treating Cal. Corp. Code section 900 or section 902 as interchangeable candidates for the source of the general power to amend is worth resolving precisely: section 900 is the section that actually grants the general power to amend articles; section 902 (the next clause) instead governs only the board-and-shareholder approval mechanics for exercising that power, not the power's existence. The two quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code section 900, and are treated as one source, not independent ones. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. This document is informational only and does not itself amend any corporation's articles.

BOARD AND SHAREHOLDER APPROVAL OF AN AMENDMENT
Once a corporation has issued any shares, California's amendment statute requires two separate approvals for an ordinary amendment of the articles, in either order: approval by the board, and approval by the outstanding shares entitled to vote under the statute's general shareholder-approval definition. Beyond that baseline majority-of-outstanding-shares rule, the statute also locks in place any higher voting threshold the articles themselves already specify: whenever the articles require a larger proportion of shares of a class or series, or a larger proportion of directors, than the statute otherwise demands, that heightened requirement cannot itself be altered, amended, or repealed except by that same heightened vote, unless the articles provide otherwise. The statute separately allows a narrow set of specific, post-issuance amendments to be adopted by board approval alone, without any shareholder vote: extending or making perpetual the existence of a corporation organized before August 14, 1929; a stock split (including a proportionate increase in authorized shares) for a corporation with only one class of shares outstanding; and deleting the same categories of original-articles historical information described in the general-power clause above.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "After any shares have been issued, amendments may be adopted if approved by the board and approved by the outstanding shares (Section 152), either before or after the approval by the board."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 902(a), California General Corporation Law, board and shareholder approval required (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=902.)
  "Whenever the articles require for corporate action the vote of a larger proportion or of all of the shares of any class or series, or of a larger proportion or of all of the directors, than is otherwise required by this division, the provision in the articles requiring such greater vote shall not be altered, amended or repealed except by such greater vote unless otherwise provided in the articles."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 902(e), California General Corporation Law, articles-based supermajority requirements are locked in (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=902.)
  Known gap: This corrects a specific assumption about where a pre-issuance, board-only amendment mechanism lives: that mechanism is a distinct, separate statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code section 901 (described in the next clause), not part of section 902. Section 902's own board-alone exceptions -- subdivisions (b), (c), and (d) -- instead apply after shares have already been issued, and only to a narrow, specifically enumerated set of amendments, not as a general "minor or technical amendment" carve-out. The two quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code section 902, and are treated as one source, not independent ones. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. This document is informational only and does not itself amend any corporation's articles.

AMENDMENT BEFORE ANY SHARES HAVE BEEN ISSUED
California's amendment statute treats a corporation that has not yet issued any shares differently from one that has. Before any shares have been issued, an amendment of the articles may be adopted simply by a signed writing, and the statute specifies who must sign it: a majority of the incorporators, if the corporation never named or elected directors, or a majority of the directors, if directors were named in the original articles or have since been elected. To make that pre-issuance amendment effective, the corporation must also file a certificate of amendment signed and verified by that same majority of incorporators or directors, stating that the signers constitute at least a majority of the incorporators or of the board, that the corporation has issued no shares, and that they adopt the amendment set out in the certificate; if the amendment was adopted by incorporators rather than directors, the certificate must also state that directors were never named in the original articles and have not been elected.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Before any shares have been issued, any amendment of the articles may be adopted by a writing signed by a majority of the incorporators, if directors were not named in the original articles and have not been elected, or, if directors were named in the original articles or have been elected, by a majority of the directors."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 901, California General Corporation Law, amendment before shares are issued (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=901.)
  "In the case of amendments adopted by the incorporators or the board under Section 901, the corporation shall file a certificate of amendment signed and verified by a majority of the incorporators or of the board, as the case may be, which shall state that the signers thereof constitute at least a majority of the incorporators or of the board, that the corporation has issued no shares and that they adopt the amendment or amendments therein set forth."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 906, California General Corporation Law, the pre-issuance certificate of amendment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=906.)
  Known gap: This corrects the assumption that a pre-issuance, no-shareholder-vote amendment mechanism lives inside Cal. Corp. Code section 902: it is in fact its own separate statutory section, section 901. It is also not accurately described as "board alone" in every case: section 901 authorizes either a majority of the incorporators or a majority of the directors to sign, depending on whether directors have been named or elected -- not the board specifically as a fixed rule. The two citations below are to two different statutory sections, section 901 and section 906, not subsections of one section, so each is treated as an independent source. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. This document is informational only and does not itself amend any corporation's articles.

REQUIRED CONTENT OF THE CERTIFICATE OF AMENDMENT
For an amendment adopted after a corporation has issued any shares, California's statute requires the corporation to file a certificate of amendment consisting of an "officers' certificate" -- a specific, defined term meaning a certificate signed and verified by one officer from one group (the chairperson of the board, the president, or any vice president) and one officer from a second group (the secretary, the chief financial officer, the treasurer, or any assistant secretary or assistant treasurer). That officers' certificate must state: the wording of the amendment or amended articles, established according to the statute's separate wording-mechanics rule; that the amendment has been approved by the board; if approval by the outstanding shares was required, that the amendment was approved by the required shareholder vote, the total number of outstanding shares of each class entitled to vote, and that the shares voting in favor equaled or exceeded the vote required, specifying the required percentage for each class; and, if the amendment was one the board could adopt alone, the facts entitling the board to do so without a shareholder vote. Separately, the statute's wording-mechanics rule requires the certificate to establish the text of the amendment in one of three ways: stating that the articles are amended to read as set forth in full, identifying an existing provision (by its designation or its wording) that is being struck or amended to read as stated, or stating that new provisions are being added.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In the case of amendments adopted after the corporation has issued any shares, the corporation shall file a certificate of amendment, which shall consist of an officers’ certificate stating: (a) The wording of the amendment or amended articles in accordance with Section 907; (b) That the amendment has been approved by the board; (c) If the amendment is one for which the approval of the outstanding shares (Section 152) is required, that the amendment was approved by the required vote of shareholders in accordance with Section 902, 903 or 904; the total number of outstanding shares of each class entitled to vote with respect to the amendment; and that the number of shares of each class voting in favor of the amendment equaled or exceeded the vote required, specifying the percentage vote required of each class entitled to vote; and (d) If the amendment is one which may be adopted with approval by the board alone, a statement of the facts entitling the board alone to adopt the amendment."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 905, California General Corporation Law, required content of the post-issuance certificate of amendment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=905.)
  "The certificate of amendment shall establish the wording of the amendment or amended articles by one or more of the following means: (1) By stating that the articles shall be amended to read as therein set forth in full. (2) By stating that any provision of the articles, which shall be identified by the numerical or other designation given it in the articles or by stating the wording thereof, shall be stricken from the articles or shall be amended to read as set forth in the certificate. (3) By stating that the provisions set forth therein shall be added to the articles."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 907(a), California General Corporation Law, how the amendment's wording must be stated (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=907.)
  "“Officers’ certificate” means a certificate signed and verified by the chairperson of the board, the president or any vice president and by the secretary, the chief financial officer, the treasurer or any assistant secretary or assistant treasurer."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 173, California General Corporation Law, definition of "officers' certificate" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=173.)
  Known gap: This corrects the assumption that the required content of the certificate of amendment is set out in Cal. Corp. Code section 906: for a corporation that has already issued shares, that content is instead governed by section 905 (what the certificate must state) together with section 907 (how the amendment's wording must be established); section 906 governs the different, pre-issuance certificate described in the clause above. The three citations below draw from three independently enacted sections -- section 905, section 907, and section 173 -- none of which is a subsection of another, so each is treated as an independent source. This is one state's list of required certificate content, not a claim about what any other state's equivalent filing must contain. This document is informational only and does not itself amend any corporation's articles.

AMENDMENTS REQUIRING A SEPARATE CLASS VOTE
California's amendment statute requires a proposed amendment to be separately approved by the outstanding shares of a particular class -- whether or not the articles otherwise give that class any vote at all -- whenever the amendment would: increase or decrease that class's aggregate authorized shares (subject to two specific statutory exceptions); effect an exchange, reclassification, or cancellation of all or part of that class's shares (a reverse stock split counts, an ordinary stock split does not); effect or create a right to exchange another class's shares into that class; change that class's rights, preferences, privileges, or restrictions; create a new class, or increase the rights, preferences, privileges, or authorized shares of an existing class, ranking ahead of that class; in the case of preferred shares, divide the class into series with different rights (or authorize the board to do so); or cancel or otherwise affect dividends that have accrued on that class but remain unpaid. Different series within the same class do not count as different classes for this class-voting purpose, unless a particular series is adversely affected by the amendment differently than other shares of the same class. This class-level approval requirement is in addition to, not instead of, the amendment's separate approval by the outstanding voting shares as a whole.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A proposed amendment must be approved by the outstanding shares (Section 152) of a class, whether or not such class is entitled to vote thereon by the provisions of the articles, if the amendment would: (1) Increase or decrease the aggregate number of authorized shares of such class, other than an increase as provided in either subdivision (b) of Section 405 or subdivision (c) of Section 902. (2) Effect an exchange, reclassification, or cancellation of all or part of the shares of such class, including a reverse stock split but excluding a stock split. (3) Effect an exchange, or create a right of exchange, of all or part of the shares of another class into the shares of such class. (4) Change the rights, preferences, privileges or restrictions of the shares of such class. (5) Create a new class of shares having rights, preferences or privileges prior to the shares of such class, or increase the rights, preferences or privileges or the number of authorized shares of any class having rights, preferences or privileges prior to the shares of such class. (6) In the case of preferred shares, divide the shares of any class into series having different rights, preferences, privileges or restrictions or authorize the board to do so. (7) Cancel or otherwise affect dividends on the shares of such class which have accrued but have not been paid."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 903(a), California General Corporation Law, amendments requiring a separate class vote (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=903.)
  "In addition to approval by a class as provided in subdivision (a), a proposed amendment must also be approved by the outstanding voting shares (Section 152)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 903(c), California General Corporation Law, class approval is in addition to overall shareholder approval (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=903.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation; whether and when a class vote is required on a charter amendment varies by state. The two quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code section 903, and are treated as one source, not independent ones. This document is informational only and does not itself amend any corporation's articles.

WHEN AN AMENDMENT BECOMES EFFECTIVE
Filing the certificate of amendment with the Secretary of State is what actually changes the articles: upon that filing, the articles are amended in accordance with the certificate, any stock split, reverse split, reclassification, cancellation, exchange, or other change to shares takes effect, and a Secretary-of-State-certified copy of the certificate becomes prima facie evidence that the conditions for adopting the amendment were satisfied. California's general corporate-filing statute separately allows a filed instrument to specify a delayed effective date up to 90 days after its filing date -- and unlike original articles of incorporation (which that delayed-effective-date mechanism expressly excludes), a certificate of amendment is exactly the kind of "instrument filed with respect to a corporation" the delayed-effective-date option is written to cover. If a delayed effective date is specified, the amendment can still be stopped before it takes effect by filing a revocation certificate, executed the same way as the original instrument, before the specified date.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Upon the filing of the certificate of amendment, the articles shall be amended in accordance with the certificate and any stock split, reverse stock split, reclassification, cancellation, exchange or other change in shares shall be effected, and a copy of the certificate, certified by the Secretary of State, is prima facie evidence of the performance of the conditions necessary to the adoption of the amendment."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 908, California General Corporation Law, effect of filing the certificate of amendment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=908.)
  "Any instrument filed with respect to a corporation, other than original articles or instruments filed pursuant to Section 119, may provide that it is to become effective not more than 90 days subsequent to its filing date. In case such a delayed effective date is specified, the instrument may be prevented from becoming effective by a certificate stating that by appropriate corporate action it has been revoked and is null and void, executed in the same manner as the original instrument and filed before the specified effective date."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 110(c), California General Corporation Law, the delayed-effective-date option for filed instruments (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=110.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation; when a filed amendment becomes effective, and whether a delayed effective date is available, vary by state. The two citations below are to two independently enacted statutory sections, Cal. Corp. Code section 908 and section 110, not subsections of one section, so each is treated as an independent source; section 110 is the same general filing-mechanics statute already used elsewhere in this corpus for the original Articles of Incorporation document's delayed-filing-date clause, and was independently re-verified here for this document. This document is informational only and does not itself amend any corporation's articles.

RESTATED ARTICLES AS AN ALTERNATIVE TO A STANDALONE CERTIFICATE OF AMENDMENT
California law gives a corporation a second, separate filing option distinct from a standalone certificate of amendment: it may consolidate its entire articles as amended into one integrated document by filing a certificate -- signed either as an officers' certificate or, in the narrower circumstances where incorporators or the board may amend the articles under the pre-issuance provisions described above, by a majority of the incorporators or the board -- titled "Restated Articles of Incorporation," setting out the articles as amended to the date of filing. That restatement can also itself amend the articles further, in which case the certificate must independently satisfy the ordinary certificate-of-amendment content and wording rules. Once filed, restated articles supersede the original articles and every amendment and certificate of determination filed before them, for all purposes -- replacing the patchwork of the original articles plus each separate amendment with one current, self-contained document, rather than adding one more standalone amendment on top of that patchwork.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A corporation may restate in a single certificate the entire text of its articles as amended by filing an officers’ certificate or, in circumstances where incorporators or the board may amend a corporation’s articles pursuant to Sections 901 and 906, a certificate signed and verified by a majority of the incorporators or the board, as applicable, entitled Restated Articles of Incorporation, which shall set forth the articles as amended to the date of the filing of the certificate"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 910(a), California General Corporation Law, filing restated articles of incorporation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=910.)
  "Restated articles of incorporation filed pursuant to this section shall supersede for all purposes the original articles and all amendments and certificates of determination filed prior thereto."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 910(d), California General Corporation Law, restated articles supersede the original articles and prior amendments (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=910.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation; whether a restated-articles mechanism exists, and its practical effect, vary by state. The two quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code section 910, and are treated as one source, not independent ones. This document is informational only and does not itself amend, restate, or supersede any corporation's articles.

OFFICER SIGNATURE AND CERTIFICATION
Executed as an officers' certificate. The undersigned certifies that they hold the office of Acme Corp shown below, that they have read the foregoing certificate of amendment, and that its contents are true of the undersigned's own knowledge.

Officer: Jordan Alex Lee, President

Signature: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

_______________________________ Date: _______________
(A second officer's signature completes an officers' certificate under Cal. Corp. Code § 173: one signer from the chairperson of the board, the president, or a vice president, and one signer from the secretary, the chief financial officer, the treasurer, or an assistant secretary or assistant treasurer.)

citations.quote: The certificate of amendment shall establish the wording of the amendment or amended articles by one or more of the following means: (1) By stating that the articles shall be amended to read as therein set forth in full. (2) By stating that any provision of the articles, which shall be identified by the numerical or other designation given it in the articles or by stating the wording thereof, shall be stricken from the articles or shall be amended to read as set forth in the certificate. (3) By stating that the provisions set forth therein shall be added to the articles.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, definition of "officers' certificate"
citations.quote: “Officers’ certificate” means a certificate signed and verified by the chairperson of the board, the president or any vice president and by the secretary, the chief financial officer, the treasurer or any assistant secretary or assistant treasurer.

expectedJSON.body: California's amendment statute requires a proposed amendment to be separately approved by the outstanding shares of a particular class -- whether or not the articles otherwise give that class any vote at all -- whenever the amendment would: increase or decrease that class's aggregate authorized shares (subject to two specific statutory exceptions); effect an exchange, reclassification, or cancellation of all or part of that class's shares (a reverse stock split counts, an ordinary stock split does not); effect or create a right to exchange another class's shares into that class; change that class's rights, preferences, privileges, or restrictions; create a new class, or increase the rights, preferences, privileges, or authorized shares of an existing class, ranking ahead of that class; in the case of preferred shares, divide the class into series with different rights (or authorize the board to do so); or cancel or otherwise affect dividends that have accrued on that class but remain unpaid. Different series within the same class do not count as different classes for this class-voting purpose, unless a particular series is adversely affected by the amendment differently than other shares of the same class. This class-level approval requirement is in addition to, not instead of, the amendment's separate approval by the outstanding voting shares as a whole.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, amendments requiring a separate class vote
citations.quote: A proposed amendment must be approved by the outstanding shares (Section 152) of a class, whether or not such class is entitled to vote thereon by the provisions of the articles, if the amendment would: (1) Increase or decrease the aggregate number of authorized shares of such class, other than an increase as provided in either subdivision (b) of Section 405 or subdivision (c) of Section 902. (2) Effect an exchange, reclassification, or cancellation of all or part of the shares of such class, including a reverse stock split but excluding a stock split. (3) Effect an exchange, or create a right of exchange, of all or part of the shares of another class into the shares of such class. (4) Change the rights, preferences, privileges or restrictions of the shares of such class. (5) Create a new class of shares having rights, preferences or privileges prior to the shares of such class, or increase the rights, preferences or privileges or the number of authorized shares of any class having rights, preferences or privileges prior to the shares of such class. (6) In the case of preferred shares, divide the shares of any class into series having different rights, preferences, privileges or restrictions or authorize the board to do so. (7) Cancel or otherwise affect dividends on the shares of such class which have accrued but have not been paid.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, class approval is in addition to overall shareholder approval
citations.quote: In addition to approval by a class as provided in subdivision (a), a proposed amendment must also be approved by the outstanding voting shares (Section 152).

expectedJSON.body: Filing the certificate of amendment with the Secretary of State is what actually changes the articles: upon that filing, the articles are amended in accordance with the certificate, any stock split, reverse split, reclassification, cancellation, exchange, or other change to shares takes effect, and a Secretary-of-State-certified copy of the certificate becomes prima facie evidence that the conditions for adopting the amendment were satisfied. California's general corporate-filing statute separately allows a filed instrument to specify a delayed effective date up to 90 days after its filing date -- and unlike original articles of incorporation (which that delayed-effective-date mechanism expressly excludes), a certificate of amendment is exactly the kind of "instrument filed with respect to a corporation" the delayed-effective-date option is written to cover. If a delayed effective date is specified, the amendment can still be stopped before it takes effect by filing a revocation certificate, executed the same way as the original instrument, before the specified date.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, effect of filing the certificate of amendment
citations.quote: Upon the filing of the certificate of amendment, the articles shall be amended in accordance with the certificate and any stock split, reverse stock split, reclassification, cancellation, exchange or other change in shares shall be effected, and a copy of the certificate, certified by the Secretary of State, is prima facie evidence of the performance of the conditions necessary to the adoption of the amendment.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the delayed-effective-date option for filed instruments
citations.quote: Any instrument filed with respect to a corporation, other than original articles or instruments filed pursuant to Section 119, may provide that it is to become effective not more than 90 days subsequent to its filing date. In case such a delayed effective date is specified, the instrument may be prevented from becoming effective by a certificate stating that by appropriate corporate action it has been revoked and is null and void, executed in the same manner as the original instrument and filed before the specified effective date.

expectedJSON.body: California law gives a corporation a second, separate filing option distinct from a standalone certificate of amendment: it may consolidate its entire articles as amended into one integrated document by filing a certificate -- signed either as an officers' certificate or, in the narrower circumstances where incorporators or the board may amend the articles under the pre-issuance provisions described above, by a majority of the incorporators or the board -- titled "Restated Articles of Incorporation," setting out the articles as amended to the date of filing. That restatement can also itself amend the articles further, in which case the certificate must independently satisfy the ordinary certificate-of-amendment content and wording rules. Once filed, restated articles supersede the original articles and every amendment and certificate of determination filed before them, for all purposes -- replacing the patchwork of the original articles plus each separate amendment with one current, self-contained document, rather than adding one more standalone amendment on top of that patchwork.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, filing restated articles of incorporation
citations.quote: A corporation may restate in a single certificate the entire text of its articles as amended by filing an officers’ certificate or, in circumstances where incorporators or the board may amend a corporation’s articles pursuant to Sections 901 and 906, a certificate signed and verified by a majority of the incorporators or the board, as applicable, entitled Restated Articles of Incorporation, which shall set forth the articles as amended to the date of the filing of the certificate

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, restated articles supersede the original articles and prior amendments
citations.quote: Restated articles of incorporation filed pursuant to this section shall supersede for all purposes the original articles and all amendments and certificates of determination filed prior thereto.
